reader.title: Lynching of Jasper Delaughter
bases: A prisoner held on a burglary charge was taken from a deputy marshal by masked men and hanged (A1, A5, A6).

A 'mob' or 'party' of masked men took an accused burglar from federal custody and hanged him (A1, A5); several men were later charged with the lynching (A5, A6). The victim's race is never stated, so whether this was anti-Black violence is unknown.

The wire brief (A1), an independent Little Rock special (A5) and a correspondent's letter (A6) agree that a prisoner was taken from federal officers by masked men and hanged, though they differ on details.

summary.text: The lynching of Jasper Delaughter was the hanging, in early October 1881, of a man under arrest for burglarizing a store in the southwestern Choctaw Nation, whom masked men took from a deputy marshal who was conveying him to Fort Smith.
Several weeks later, officers from Fort Smith arrested a number of residents of Sevier County, Arkansas, including a physician, on charges of taking part in the lynching.
None of the reports stated the race of Delaughter or of the men accused.
According to a brief news item that ran in early October, Delaughter was under arrest for burglarizing the store of T. J. Wright in the southwestern part of the Choctaw Nation.
A Little Rock special to the Memphis Daily Appeal, dated November 2, gave the storekeeper's name as J. D. Wright, placed the store near Cerro Gordo, and said it had been robbed and destroyed by fire.
The same dispatch, which spelled the prisoner's name "Delaughton," said he had been arrested for the offense in Sevier County, Arkansas.
While being conveyed to Fort Smith, Delaughter was taken from the deputy marshal and "hanged by a mob of masked men," in the words of the October item.
The Little Rock dispatch said that "a party of masked men" took the prisoner from his guards and lynched him.
A correspondent of the Russellville Democrat placed the seizure in Sevier County, describing a prisoner "taken from a United States marshal in that county and hung."
No report gave the date, the time of day or the place of the hanging.

By early November, officers from Fort Smith had arrested Dr. Roberts, McElroy, Collier and "other prominent citizens of Sevier," charged with the lynching, and the Appeal's correspondent added that "considerable apprehension" was felt for the result.

The Russellville Democrat's correspondent, passing on a letter from a relative in Texarkana, wrote that several men in Sevier County had been arrested and carried to Fort Smith "with a view of prosecuting the lynchers."
No report of an indictment, trial or verdict appears in the coverage.

The first account was a single sentence in a column of general news, printed in identical wording by the Huntsville Gazette on October 8, the Batesville Guard of Arkansas on October 12, the Iron County Register of Ironton, Missouri, on October 13, and the Iola Register of Kansas on October 14.
The item named no race and offered no comment on the mob.

The Memphis Daily Appeal gave the arrests more pointed treatment, running the Little Rock dispatch under a subheading that, through heavy OCR errors, reads as "Arkansas Authorities Have Taken a Right Step" and urges them to follow it up.
In Arkansas, the Russellville Democrat mentioned the arrests only in passing, within a correspondent's column of Dover news, and did not name the victim.
The accounts differ on details: the October item named the storekeeper T. J. Wright and described a burglary, while the Little Rock dispatch named J. D. Wright and said the store was also burned.

The October item had Delaughter taken from the deputy marshal en route to Fort Smith, the dispatch said he was taken from "the guards," and the Russellville correspondent placed the seizure in Sevier County.
